https://metro.co.uk/2026/09/23/8-newest-.text: The ‘O’ in October stands for Out of Office (Picture: Shutterstock / kavalenkau) If you’re a Londoner looking for a new favourite holiday destination, keep reading. From next month, a string of airlines will be dropping new flights to Europe and beyond — all taking off from your doorstep. So, whether you fancy a short and sweet weekend in Spain or a tropical Caribbean adventure, there are plenty of routes to choose from. All that’s left to do now is convince your boss to grant that last-minute annual leave… London Heathrow to Phuket, Thailand Thailand continues to be one of the most popular long-haul destinations for Brits. The crown jewel of Southeast Asian tourism, it’s loved for backpacking, culture, and winter sun. This is your sign to book tickets to Thailand (Picture: Shutterstock / Arkadij Schell) Phuket is the most-visited island for British tourists (alongside Koh Samui and Phi Phi), so it makes sense that Virgin Atlantic is jumping on the bandwagon and launching its first-ever direct flight from London. From October 18, travellers can fly straight to Thailand’s largest island from Heathrow, where flights will operate on Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays. Return flights to the UK will then run on Thursdays, Saturdays and Mondays, departing at 9.20am and landing at 4pm. Currently, Heathrow passengers typically face at least two flights — stopping over in either Beijing, Shanghai, or Kuala Lumpur — and a journey time of anywhere between 17 and 22 hours. The new route is expected to take around 13 hours. One-way fares start from £647. London Gatwick to Colombo, Sri Lanka Sri Lanka was named in many 2026 trending destination roundups, from Lonely Planet to Time Out to Condé Nast Traveller. @dypnnz 2 weeks itinerary Sri Lanka : 2 days Sigirya 1 day Kandy 3 days Ella 3 days Arugam Bay 1 day Yala national park 2 days Mirissa 1 day Galle 1 day Colombo #srilanka #travelitinerary #colombo #mirissa #kandy ♬ Maphupho Fezeka – FRENCH FUSE The South Asian country has multiple UNESCO World Heritage sites, including ancient cities like Anuradhapura and the rock fortress of Sigiriya. It also boasts superstar beaches and a rich culinary heritage. Earlier this year, British Airways announced a major winter expansion — including adding Colombo, Sri Lanka’s capital, as a new destination. The route will launch on October 23 and feature three 10-hour flights per week. Economy return fares start from £620. Travellers note: the Gatwick to Colombo service will only run during the winter season, with the final inbound flight scheduled for March 27, 2027. So, if you’re in the market for a Sri Lankan getaway, get booking now. London Gatwick to Barbados The Caribbean island of Barbados was on Lonely Planet’s Best in Travel list for 2026. Cocktails in the Caribbean, anyone? (Picture: Shutterstock / zstock) With its UNESCO World Heritage Site capital, Bridgetown, and award-winning beaches, the island also boasts a vibrant ‘Culinary Capital’ food scene, fusing Caribbean and African flavours. Not that we need to tempt you further, but British Airways has new direct daily flights from October 25. Return economy flights start from £522, and the journey time is eight and a half hours. This service complements BA’s existing year-round flights from London Heathrow and will feature onward connections to Grenada, Guyana, and Tobago. London Heathrow to Costa Rica Dreaming of misty cloud forests, cascading jungle waterfalls and palm-fringed white sand beaches? Costa Rica might be the destination for you. @natfernandez.co Dreaming about this place 💚🌴✨ #costarica #traveltiktok ♬ original sound – Directorschair It’s one of the most popular spots in Central America, especially for eco-tourists. From October 2026, BA’s flights from Costa Rica will depart from London Heathrow instead of London Gatwick. Flights to the capital, San José, will run five times a week during the winter season and three times a week in the summer, operating as a year-round service starting on October 25. Return flights in economy class start from £654 in November and will take 11 hours. London Heathrow to Tampa Like the Costa Rica flight, BA’s service to Tampa, Florida, will swap London airports. The route used to take off from Gatwick; however, from October 25, they’ll run from Heathrow. @amyenvoyage Planning a Florida trip? Save this for later 📍AD Comment ‘TAMPA BAY’ and I’ll send you my full guide with where to stay, eat and the best things to do. Before visiting, I had no idea one destination was home to wild chickens roaming the streets, rescued manatees, America’s oldest family-owned premium cigar maker and the world’s largest Spanish restaurant. There is so much variety. You can spend the morning exploring historic neighbourhoods, the afternoon out on the water and the evening discovering an incredible food scene, rooftop bars and waterfront restaurants. And it’s really easy to get to from the UK too. You can fly direct from London to Tampa, or if you’re already visiting Orlando, it’s around a 1.5–2 hour drive away. You can bag nine-hour return flights from as little as £450, with average prices never really changing throughout the year. Once you’ve landed in Tampa, relax on pristine beaches, try a Tampa Cuban sandwich, go parasailing, or experience the vibrant nightlife. Luton to Malaga, Granada and Asturias, Spain Don’t have enough annual leave for a long-haul trip? Turn your attention to Wizz Air’s new Spanish routes from London Luton. Launching in late October 2026 (25 for Malaga, and 27 for Granada and Asturias), the services will operate all year round. Malaga flights will take off four times a week, Granada will operate twice weekly, and Asturias will get three flights per week. Managing director at Wizz Air UK, Yvonne Moynihan, said of the launches: ‘Spain has always been one of the UK’s favourite holiday destinations, and we’re excited to be expanding our Spanish network with three more fantastic routes from London Luton Airport. ‘Whether customers are planning a beach break on the Costa del Sol, a cultural escape to Granada, or looking to discover the stunning landscapes of Asturias, we’re making it even easier for our customers to enjoy more of Spain, for less.’ Even more exciting? Tickets won’t break the bank, with one-way fares starting from £17.99. London Stansted to La Palma Keen for some winter sun closer to home? Add La Palma in the Canary Islands to your bucket list. @saltinourhair Unfortunately, this island ruined our definition of adventure in Europe forever… 🥹🌋 🧡 Follow @saltinourhair for more Unique destinations, hidden gems and itineraries💕 Volcanic landscapes, black-sand beaches, natural pools, and some of the most incredible hikes we’ve ever done. Because we can now confirm: 100% worth the trip 😍 Some our favorites on La Palma: 🌺 Ruta de los Volcanos hike 🌺 Poris de Candelaria (with sunset) 🌺 Playa de Nogales (with sunrise) 🌺 Pozas Naturales de Achentive 🌺 La Papaya (for Brunch) Save this Reel for planning later! — Best things to do La Palma | La Palma itinerary | Canary Islands Spain | Hidden gems Europe ♬ original sound – Salt in our Hair La Palma is often described as the Canary Islands’ ‘best-kept secret’, and is home to forested terrain, narrow cobbled streets and glistening turquoise water. There’s a huge focus on nature here: hike the Ruta de los Volcanes, Caldera de Taburiente National Park, or Cubo de la Galga, an ancient laurel forest and UNESCO World Biosphere Reserve. On the water, La Palma boasts plenty of natural pools, including Charco Azul and Piscinas de la Fajana, both in the northeast of the island. The beauty spots are available to visit free of charge. As for how to get there, Jet2.com is launching a new route from London Stansted on October 26, with one-way fares starting from £30. London Southend to Budapest, Hungary Finally, if you’re more of a city breaker, may we direct you to easyJet’s brand-new Southend to Budapest route. If you’ve still to tick Budapest off your bucket list, now’s your chance (Picture: Shutterstock / Mistervlad) Heading to the Hungarian capital on October 26, either book an autumn getaway or schedule a festive weekend in December. Budapest is well-known for being cracking at Christmas, after all. The service will run on Mondays and Fridays, from £24 one-way. Or, book a Jet2 package break from £260 per person. While you’re in Budapest, relax in the outdoor and indoor Thermal Baths, take a Danube River cruise, or drink in one of the ‘ruin’ pubs scattered throughout the historic Jewish Quarter.

Illustration: John Kazior View image in fullscreen The Lónyay–Hatvany-villa, headquarters of the Danube Institute, in Budapest. Illustration: John Kazior The long read Hungary ‘The last bastion is gone’: the US right idolised Orbán’s Hungary. Can they recover now he has fallen? Over the past decade, Hungary has been a beacon for the ‘postliberal’ right, with pro-Trump thinkers making regular pilgrimages to Budapest. Now Orbán is gone, how will the movement adapt? A longer version of this article first appeared in The Drift Brian Goodman Tue 20 Oct 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 05.47 EDT Share Espresso Embassy, a third-wave coffee shop in Budapest’s diplomatic and governmental quarter, is where visiting reporters and academics come to talk politics. On the way in for my morning coffee on 18 March, I passed a poster for Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party that had been vandalised with a marker pen: “the safe choice” had become “the certain way to get fucked”. From across the cafe, I spotted the American journalist and historian Anne Applebaum locked in conversation, possibly with a source. I heard someone exclaim: “Just like Mussolini!” It was election season in Hungary. It was also a couple of days before Cpac Hungary , a satellite event of the US-based conservative conference. As members of the international right arrived in town, the notorious Orbánist thinktank known as the Danube Institute was hosting an event called On Censorship, Tolerance, the Left and God. The official line would be: bad, good, bad, good. After dark, I walked along the walls of Buda castle and past the Jesuit stairs to the institute. The featured speakers were Dave Rubin, an American podcaster from the so-called “intellectual dark web”, and Eva Vlaardingerbroek, a Dutch provocateur who claimed the title “shieldmaiden of the far right” on her X profile. “You don’t realise how good you have it” in Hungary , Rubin said. “So many things are wrong across the west.” After the panel, an American man introduced himself to me and asked how long I’d been in Budapest. Had I ever considered dual citizenship? If so, he could help. “My friends,” he said, “call me the Harriet Tubman of white people.” For the previous few months, I’d been hanging around the Danube Institute and other state-subsidised gathering places, trying to pass as yet another member of the rightwing intelligentsia making his pilgrimage to Budapest. Founded in 2013 with state funds redirected by the Orbán government, the institute had become known as the central hub in the emerging “postliberal” movement, a loose coalition of heterodox conservative thinkers frequently associated with the idiosyncratic American blogger and self-styled Christian dissident Rod Dreher. During Dreher’s first fellowship term at the Danube Institute in 2021, he helped arrange Tucker Carlson’s weeklong press junket in Hungary, which featured a fawning Fox News interview with Orbán. Since then, liberal publications such as the New York Times, the New Yorker and the Atlantic have dispatched journalists to grill Dreher about the institute and his relationship to Orbán’s autocratic regime. This produced a series of breathless reports that showcased the small thinktank as a clearinghouse for dangerous illiberal ideas. As Applebaum wrote in her book Twilight of Democracy : “The Danube Institute exists, in practice, to make the Hungarian government presentable to the outside world.” In Applebaum’s view, the Orbán regime had “created a political system in which no opposition party could possibly win”, and the foreign intellectuals at the Danube Institute were either cynical propagandists or naive stooges for Orbán’s anti-democratic project. But soon, Orbán would be out of power, ousted in a landslide election in April , and in June the new Hungarian parliament would pass a constitutional amendment dismantling the patronage system that funds the Danube Institute, as well as MCC Brussels , a training ground for Fidesz elites. It was end times for the postliberals in Budapest, even if they didn’t know it yet. What will survive the demise of the so-called Budapest scene is a fractured group of rightwing thinkers who, whatever their fate in Hungary, will continue to hold a frightening level of influence over US political culture. If they were ever Orbán’s puppets, they aren’t any more. But reducing them to the unthinking servants of one particular strongman has made it more difficult to confront the real threat of postliberal ideas – or the crisis to which they are responding. Officially, I was in Budapest to write a book about the western intellectuals who travelled to Hungary to meet the dissident opposition during the final years of the communist era. My family and I were guests of the Institute for Advanced Study, which had once been called the Collegium Budapest before it was effectively closed by the Orbán government in 2011. Now reopened, it was part of the rump of Central European University that still remained in Hungary. The rest of the institution was forced to move to Vienna during a prolonged campaign against George Soros and Hungary’s independent civil society. At the start of this year, I made it my half-ironic mission to infiltrate the Danube Institute. I really did want to see what was actually going on inside this thinktank that had become known as the headquarters of the international postliberal project. Reaching it was not hard. It is housed in the Lónyay-Hatvany Villa, a refurbished building that had briefly served as an SS casino during the second world war and now housed a high-end restaurant on its main floor. One evening, I climbed a steep staircase dimly lit by iron sconces, the yellow light reflecting off wet stone, until I reached a narrow passage closed in by two high walls. Up ahead, I noticed a doorway marked only by a floor lamp on a small red carpet. I hesitated, then entered. View image in fullscreen Péter Magyar celebrates his Tisza party’s victory in the Hungarian general election in April. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock Straight in front of me was a dining room with a commanding view of the Danube. I snapped a few photos with my phone until I heard someone behind me on the stairs. I hurried into the basement annexe and reached a check-in table. I gave a young assistant my name, and she pointed towards a coat check. It turned out that infiltrating the Danube Institute just required online registration. In the brightly lit basement, a shelf offered complimentary issues of glossy rightwing journals such as The European Conservative and Hungarian Review. I picked up a copy of the then state-subsidised Hungarian Conservative with a painting by Tivadar Csontváry Kosztka on the cover; its title was Mysterious Island. The other guests were beginning to arrive, and I was immediately worried I’d been misled by a New Yorker piece on Dreher, in which he told a journalist that “the Danube Institute had a casual dress code” and he “could usually leave the suits at the apartment” even when meeting with ministers from Orbán’s Fidesz party. But here was a parade of male intellectual fashion: ribbed turtlenecks; crocheted ties and silk cravats; blazers of tweed, linen and corduroy. I looked down at my rumpled blazer – the only one I own – and felt underdressed. In the months to come, I would jot down scraps of overheard conversation. Much of it was unsurprising, especially for anyone who had spent time on X: “We’re going to interrogate him with truth serum”, “No one is linking except Tucker”, “Hitler would have gone broke on her OnlyFans”, “Do you have a contact for Vance?” All the knowing gossip and memes were part of a game of one-upmanship among intellectuals who styled themselves as insiders. Still, there was something jarring about seeing this very online culture in the flesh. Most of the names they dropped were exactly the ones you’d expect. What did catch me off guard was how often I also heard them mention the names of the liberal journalists who had alerted me to the existence of the Danube Institute in the first place. If Hungary looms large for people like Applebaum, she, in turn, haunts the postliberal imagination; these guys all clearly read the Atlantic. “Anne Applebaum, I think she’s great,” I overheard one of the institute’s fellows wisecrack at the bar. “I really respect her.” At the very first event I attended, a debate on How Non-Liberal Regimes Rule Through the Good Life, the main speaker referred to Applebaum as “persona non grata” at the Danube Institute. The postliberal economist Philip Pilkington responded: “I do find the descent into Applebaumism hilarious.” Pilkington was referring to Applebaum’s stubborn tendency to divide the world between liberal democracies and illiberal autocracies, between virtuous and corrupt elites. This “moral purity test” was not only hypocritical, he pointed out, it was intellectually unserious. According to Pilkington, it prevented liberal elites from accurately seeing themselves. The “crude” Applebaum analysis, he said, doesn’t “have a good explanation of why liberalism is falling apart”. Part of the appeal of postliberalism is that it does provide an account of why it feels as though everything is falling apart: a liberal world order could never have turned out otherwise. At least this is Pilkington’s view, as expressed in his 2025 book, The Collapse of Global Liberalism. Born in Ireland, Pilkington is a millennial former leftist who took a job in finance and then moved to Hungary, where until June he was employed at the Danube Institute and the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, then another Fidesz-aligned thinktank. For him, “liberalism is, in the final analysis, a dark and uncivilised philosophy of life that will destroy any civilisation it touches”. Equally comfortable making sweeping claims about “Marxian historical materialism” and offering hot takes about yoga pants as a symptom of civilisational decline, Pilkington argues that the drive to demolish all hierarchies is “self-undermining” and “self-destructive”: “The reality is that equality does not exist in most spheres.” Liberal capitalism, according to this line of thought, only ever appeared stable because it was built on a foundation of pre-liberal hierarchical structures, such as the church, family and classical legal traditions. Now it has become a victim of its own self-undermining success. As Pilkington puts it, “liberal capitalism” became “far too aggressive in its promotion of work and consumption and is undermining the building blocks on which the stability of society rests”, namely “the family and the ability to reproduce the species”. The postliberal movement’s foundational text is 2018’s Why Liberalism Failed by the philosopher Patrick Deneen, another visitor to the Danube Institute. The title of Deneen’s book captures the shared premise of all postliberal thought: that the historical period in which western societies were governed by a “regime of liberalism”, as he put it elsewhere, has already reached a calamitous end. Whether that period began in 1989 with the fall of communist regimes in central and eastern Europe or 500 years ago with the Protestant reformation remains a matter of some obfuscation. For postliberals, the collapse of liberalism was an inevitable outgrowth of its first principles: its anti-hierarchical commitment to formal equality, its faith in human progress and, above all, its emphasis on individual autonomy. In practice, Deneen argues, these values actually produced extreme economic inequality, spiritual debasement and a profound sense of unfreedom. “Liberalism has failed,” he writes, “not because it fell short, but because it was true to itself.” View image in fullscreen Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, on stage at Cpac Hungary in March. Photograph: Gergely Besenyei/AFP/Getty Images At least initially, the postliberals seemed more solicitous of the populist masses than of the Republican old guard: they supported Donald Trump, who was then styling himself as a champion for a new working-class coalition against the elite establishment. Deneen and other postliberals claimed their goal was to transcend the toxic left-right divide in US politics by positioning themselves as both allies of social democracy and enemies of corporate progressivism. Indeed, they insisted the only way to defeat the disastrous post-cold war alliance between neoliberal economics and neoconservative foreign policy was through a novel fusion of social-conservative values and left economic ideas. After postliberalism relocated to Hungary it became more true to itself. The year after its publication, Why Liberalism Failed was translated into Hungarian, and Deneen met Orbán in Budapest. In the years after 2018, the Danube Institute and other regime-supported institutions hosted nearly every major American postliberal intellectual in Budapest. Many are now familiar figures on the so-called New Right. To use a basketball analogy, if Deneen was the philosopher-coach and Dreher was the veteran point guard on this postliberal squad, the rest of the starting five might include the Catholic integralist Adrian Vermeule; the national conservative Yoram Hazony; the censorious culture warrior Christopher Rufo; and the shapeshifting opinion columnist, UnHerd editor and Compact magazine cofounder Sohrab Ahmari, with the political theorist Gladden Pappin coming in off the bench. Back in the US, Pappin had been a junior academic before he began writing blog posts for the Journal of American Greatness under the pen name Manlius Capitolinus. By now, all of Pappin’s posts as Manlius Capitolinus have been taken down, but he subsequently published a series of revealing essays under his own name in another journal. In Toward a Party of the State, from 2019, Pappin argued that the “liberal conservatism” of the old Republican establishment had failed precisely because it became a handmaid to the “governing ideology of neoliberalism”, a form of statecraft without a moral vision of the good life. Drawing on left thinkers such as Nancy Fraser , Pappin suggested that neoliberalism maintained its fragile legitimacy by “redefining itself as progressive”, creating an unholy alliance between pro-corporate and socially liberal constituencies. To overcome the “neoliberal ideological hegemony”, according to this theory, we need a national unity government with a strong, activist party-state led by intellectuals, among them, presumably, Pappin himself. At the time, postliberals could still squint and see Trump as a vessel for this project. After Trump’s defeat in 2020, Pappin visited Budapest for the first time, and before long, he had relocated to Hungary. In 2023, he was appointed president of the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, a highly unusual position for a foreign national. Pappin now had the opportunity to learn from the Fidesz party-state and start putting his ideas into practice. To postliberals, Orbán’s governing programme looked like a dream come true. As Rufo, coming off his stint at the Danube Institute, put it in 2023: “Hungary’s leaders are serious people combating the same forces confronted by conservatives in the west: the fraying of national culture, entrenched leftwing institutions and the rejection of sexual difference.” But, compared with the contemporary Republican party, Orbán seemed exhilaratingly willing to use the power of the state to pursue a conservative vision of the good life.
